items.title: Fake Compliance / Internal Audit Request Pretext
items.prerequisites: Written authorization covering pretext testing that impersonates an internal compliance, legal, or audit function, with client sign-off on which department(s) may be targeted and explicit agreement on what category of data may be requested (fabricated/canary data only — never a request that would actually succeed in extracting real sensitive records). Familiarity with the organization's actual compliance/audit cadence (e.g., known annual audit periods) gathered from public filings or client-provided context, to make the pretext timing plausible.
items.whatItIs: This pretext impersonates an internal compliance, legal, or internal-audit team to request sensitive information or system access from an employee. It works because employees are naturally deferential to audit-sounding requests, and real audit requests genuinely do sometimes ask for unusual or broad information on short notice — making a fake one hard to distinguish from a real one.
items.rootCause: Employees usually have no trained, reliable way to tell a genuine internal-audit or compliance request apart from a made-up one — both look the same on the surface: an internally-styled email or call, some policy or regulatory language, a bit of time pressure. And no one expects an independent verification step before complying.
items.impact: A successful pretext extracts sensitive data — HR records, financial data, credentials requested 'for audit purposes' — or induces a policy exception such as a temporary access grant. The employee believes throughout that they are meeting a legitimate compliance obligation. Because genuine compliance requests are often legitimately broad, this pretext can yield more in one interaction than several narrower phishing attempts.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm scope, target department(s), and the exact category of fabricated/canary data or access that may be requested, ensuring the pretext can never actually succeed in obtaining real sensitive data.

Research the organization's actual compliance/audit cadence and terminology (e.g., known frameworks they're certified against, typical audit timing) from public sources or client-provided context to maximize pretext plausibility.

Identify the internal function being impersonated (internal audit, legal, a specific compliance team) and a plausible reason for the outreach (a recurring control review, a regulatory deadline, a sampling request).
Determine whether the organization has any stated verification expectation for compliance/audit requests (e.g., 'always routed through a ticketing system') as the specific control being tested.
Select a target role where the requested (fabricated) information would plausibly reside, to keep the pretext realistic and narrowly scoped to the agreed test data category.

Prepare a fallback response for if the target asks to verify through the real internal audit team's known channel, since immediate, graceful compliance with a verification request is expected and correct tester behavior.
exploitationSteps: Contact the target via email or phone, introducing the pretext as an internal audit/compliance representative conducting a routine or regulatory-driven review.
Request only the pre-agreed category of fabricated/canary information or a simulated access grant, framed as a standard part of the stated review.
Observe whether the target verifies the request (checking an internal directory, calling the real compliance team's known number/ticketing system) before complying.
If the target requests verification, comply immediately, confirm the test is authorized if pressed by the real department, and record this as the control working correctly.

If the target proceeds to comply without verification, stop at the point where compliance is confirmed — do not have them actually transmit any real sensitive data even in the test flow — and immediately disclose to the engagement contact.
Document whether the organization has a real, known internal-audit verification channel at all, since its absence is itself a finding independent of whether any individual target complied.

examplePayloads.label: Internal-audit outreach opening (email or phone)
examplePayloads.command: Hi [Name], I'm reaching out from Internal Audit as part of our quarterly access-control review — I'll need a few details from your team to complete this cycle's sample testing.

examplePayloads.label: Regulatory-deadline framing
examplePayloads.command: This is tied to our upcoming [framework] certification renewal, so we're on a tight timeline to close out this sample — appreciate your help getting this back to us today if possible.

examplePayloads.label: Fabricated/canary data request (specific, pre-agreed category only)
examplePayloads.command: Could you send over the current access list for [test-designated system], along with last review date? This is for our standard sampling documentation.

examplePayloads.label: Response if the target asks to verify
examplePayloads.command: Absolutely, happy for you to confirm — feel free to check with [real compliance team name] or route it through the usual ticketing process if that's easier on your end.

examplePayloads.label: Graceful acceptance of a firm decline
examplePayloads.command: No problem at all, I understand — I'll follow up through the standard audit-request process instead. Thanks for your time.

examplePayloads.label: Follow-up nudge (mild, non-coercive)
examplePayloads.command: Just a gentle follow-up on this when you get a chance — no rush, just want to make sure it's on your radar before the review window closes.

variants: Fake external-regulator pretext, impersonating a government or industry regulatory body rather than an internal function, typically carrying more implied authority and urgency.
Fake data-privacy/subject-access-request pretext, impersonating a legal/privacy function processing a fabricated data-subject request to extract records about a specific (test-designated) individual.
Fake insurance/cyber-liability-audit pretext, requesting security-control documentation or configuration details under the guise of a policy-renewal audit.
Phone-based (vishing) variant of the same pretext, testing whether verbal authority framing is more or less effective than the written/email form for this specific department.
mitigation: Establish and publicize a single, known, verifiable channel (a ticketing system or a named, directory-listed internal audit contact) through which all legitimate compliance/audit requests are routed, and train staff to expect and require it.
Train employees that internal audit, legal, and compliance requests are just as subject to verification as any other sensitive request — authority framing alone is not verification.

Require any request for access grants or sensitive data 'for audit purposes' to go through the same formal access-request/change-control process as any other request, with no compliance-labeled shortcut.
Maintain an internal directory that makes it easy for any employee to independently look up and confirm a claimed internal-audit or compliance contact.

Include this specific pretext category in security-awareness training, since employees are typically well-trained against generic phishing but rarely against an authority-themed internal impersonation.
Periodically test this control as part of the ongoing awareness program, not just a single point-in-time assessment, given how plausible and low-suspicion this pretext naturally is.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A request that appears to come from compliance, legal or internal audit is unusually effective, because staff are trained not to obstruct those functions and asking questions feels like non-cooperation. This finding covers whether staff would hand over sensitive information or grant access to someone invoking that authority. The remedy is to make the genuine process recognisable and the unusual one obvious: real audit and compliance requests come through a named channel, staff are told what that channel is, and anything arriving outside it is verified regardless of how official it looks. State clearly that verifying an audit request is never treated as obstruction — that single sentence removes most of the pressure the attack relies on.

reference.standard: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 - Control 14 (Security Awareness and Skills Training)
tools: Authorized spoofable sender identity (email or caller-ID, per client agreement)
Canary/fabricated test-data records prepared in advance with the client
links: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 - Control 14
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - AT-2 (Literacy Training and Awareness)

items.title: MFA Bypass via Adversary-in-the-Middle Phishing and Push Fatigue
items.prerequisites: Written authorisation naming the target population and explicitly covering credential and session-token capture, since a successful test yields live authenticated sessions. A reverse-proxy phishing framework (Evilginx, Modlishka) or an equivalent purpose-built harness, plus a registered look-alike domain and a valid TLS certificate for it. Agreement with the client on where captured session material is stored, who may access it, and when it is destroyed. A named client contact reachable during testing to halt the exercise immediately if it affects live operations.
items.whatItIs: Traditional phishing captures a password, which multi-factor authentication then blocks. These two techniques defeat that. In an adversary-in-the-middle attack the phishing site is a live reverse proxy: it relays the victim's input to the real login page in real time, so the genuine MFA prompt appears, the victim satisfies it, and the attacker captures the resulting session cookie rather than the password — a token that is already past MFA. Push fatigue is cruder: with a password already in hand, the attacker triggers approval prompts repeatedly until the target approves one to stop the interruptions.
items.rootCause: Most MFA methods prove that a valid factor was presented at some moment, not that the person approving is the person actually signing in, and not that the session belongs to the device that completed the challenge. A one-time code or a push approval is a shared secret in transit, so anything positioned between the user and the identity provider can relay it. Push notifications compound this by asking for approval with no context about where the request originated, and by allowing unlimited retries — which converts an authentication control into an interruption the user is motivated to dismiss.
items.impact: The attacker obtains an authenticated session that has already cleared MFA, so re-prompting does not stop them and a password reset alone does not evict them. That typically grants mailbox access, single-sign-on reach into every connected application, and the ability to register a new MFA method of their own for durable persistence. Because the session was established through the genuine identity provider, sign-in logs show a successful, fully-compliant authentication for the real user — which is precisely why this class routinely goes undetected until damage surfaces elsewhere.
stepsToIdentify: Establish which MFA methods the organisation actually permits, and specifically whether phishing-resistant options (FIDO2 or hardware security keys) are enforced or merely offered alongside weaker ones.
Determine whether number matching, geographic context, or application context is displayed in push approvals, since their absence is what makes push fatigue viable.
Check whether there is any limit on how many approval prompts a single sign-in attempt can generate, and whether repeated denials trigger an alert or lockout.
Review conditional-access rules for device compliance or managed-device requirements, which can block a proxied session even when credentials and MFA are captured.
Confirm whether the identity provider binds session tokens to a device or client certificate, since token binding defeats replay of a stolen cookie.

Assess detection capability: ask whether impossible-travel, new-device, and anomalous-token alerts exist and are actually reviewed, since this attack produces a legitimate-looking sign-in and detection is the fallback control.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, the target list, and the agreed halt procedure in writing before standing anything up, and verify that the look-alike domain will not be mistaken for a genuine service outside the engagement.
Stand up the reverse proxy against a test account first and validate the full capture chain end to end, so the technique is proven before any real employee is contacted.

Send the lure to the agreed population only, and record delivery, click, credential-entry and MFA-completion rates as separate figures — they measure different controls and conflate badly when merged.
On capturing a session token, verify it works with a single minimal read-only action that only confirms authentication, then stop; do not browse mailboxes or documents.

For the push-fatigue component, agree a strict prompt ceiling in advance, target a small number of consenting participants rather than the general population, and stop at the first approval or the ceiling.
Destroy captured session tokens and credentials at the end of the engagement, ask the client to revoke the affected sessions and rotate credentials, and confirm both in writing.

examplePayloads.label: Reverse-proxy phishing harness (illustrative invocation)
examplePayloads.command: evilginx2 -p ./phishlets   # then: phishlets hostname <service> login.<lookalike-domain>; phishlets enable <service>

examplePayloads.label: Look-alike domain candidates to test detection
examplePayloads.command: login-<brand>.com  ·  <brand>-sso.com  ·  <brand>.secure-login.com

examplePayloads.label: Lure framing (session-expiry pretext)
examplePayloads.command: Your session expired during scheduled maintenance. Re-authenticate within 2 hours to avoid mailbox interruption: https://login.<lookalike-domain>/

examplePayloads.label: Verify a captured session without touching data
examplePayloads.command: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Cookie: <captured-session>' https://<service>/api/me

examplePayloads.label: Push-fatigue trigger (authorised, capped)
examplePayloads.command: # Re-submit valid credentials at a fixed interval, hard-capped at the agreed prompt limit, then stop regardless of outcome.

examplePayloads.label: Check whether number matching is enforced
examplePayloads.command: # Initiate a sign-in and record whether the prompt displays a code the user must type, or only Approve/Deny.

variants: Device-code phishing, where the victim is asked to enter a legitimate device code on the real provider's page — no look-alike domain is needed, so domain-reputation defences do not apply.
Consent phishing, which requests OAuth application permissions instead of credentials, producing durable access via a token grant that survives password resets entirely.
MFA-fatigue combined with a follow-up vishing call impersonating IT to talk the target through approving the prompt, which substantially raises the success rate.
QR-code delivery of the proxy link, moving the click onto a personal phone that sits outside corporate email filtering and endpoint controls.
mitigation: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 or hardware security keys) for all privileged accounts and, where feasible, everyone — the credential is bound to the origin, so a proxy cannot relay it.
Require number matching and display application and location context in every push approval, which removes the blind Approve button that push fatigue depends on.
Bind session tokens to a compliant, managed device via conditional access, so a stolen cookie is unusable from attacker infrastructure.
Rate-limit approval prompts per sign-in attempt and alert on repeated denials, which is a reliable and specific indicator of an active push-fatigue attempt.
Monitor for impossible travel, new-device sign-ins, and anomalous token use, since this attack yields a legitimate-looking authentication that only behavioural signals will surface.
Train staff on the specific instruction that an unexpected MFA prompt should be denied and reported, never approved to make it stop — and make reporting one tap, with no blame attached.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Multi-factor authentication is no longer sufficient on its own. Two techniques defeat it in ordinary use: relaying the login through an attacker-controlled page so the approved session is stolen rather than the password, and simply sending approval prompts repeatedly until a tired user taps accept. Both were effective here, which means an attacker with a stolen password is not stopped by the second factor you have deployed. The fix is to move the accounts that matter most — administrators, finance, executives — onto phishing-resistant authentication such as hardware security keys or passkeys, which cannot be relayed. Where that is not yet possible, switch push approval to number matching and limit repeated prompts. This should be among your highest priorities.

tools: Identity provider sign-in logs for detection assessment
links: CWE-1021 (Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames)
MITRE ATT&CK T1621 (Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation)

items.title: Synthetic Voice and Video Impersonation of Executives (Deepfake-Assisted Pretexting)
items.prerequisites: Explicit written authorisation from an executive whose likeness or voice will be synthesised, obtained separately from general engagement authorisation, since this involves creating a synthetic representation of a real, identifiable person. A narrowly scoped target list and a defined financial or access request that will be halted before completion. Publicly available recordings of the impersonated executive (conference talks, earnings calls, interviews). Agreement on destruction of all synthetic media at engagement end, and a legal review, since synthetic likeness is regulated differently across jurisdictions.
items.whatItIs: Voice cloning now requires only seconds of reference audio, and real-time video synthesis is viable on consumer hardware. This removes the strongest instinctive authenticity check people have: recognising a familiar voice or face. A finance employee who would question an emailed wire request will often act on what appears to be a live call from their CFO, and the request arrives with the urgency and authority that made the pretext plausible in the first place. Real-world losses in the tens of millions have followed from single video calls with multiple synthetic participants.
items.rootCause: Approval processes are built around recognising a person rather than verifying a channel, and voice and face were historically expensive to forge convincingly. That assumption no longer holds, but the processes that depend on it have not been rewritten. Compounding this, executives publish large volumes of high-quality reference audio and video through entirely legitimate activity, so the raw material is freely available. Organisations also rarely define an out-of-band verification step for high-value requests, leaving 'it sounded like him' as the operative control.
items.impact: The immediate impact is fraudulent payment or unauthorised access granted through a process that behaved exactly as designed, because the authorisation appeared to come from a recognised person. Beyond the direct loss, a successful synthetic impersonation undermines every voice-based verification the organisation relies on — help-desk identity checks, verbal payment approvals, and executive instructions — and there is no straightforward technical fix that restores them. Recovery of funds after a same-day wire transfer is rare, so prevention and process design carry essentially all of the weight.
stepsToIdentify: Assess how much high-quality reference audio and video of key executives is publicly available, since that determines how convincing a synthetic impersonation could be and is itself a reportable exposure.
Map every process where a verbal or video instruction alone can authorise a payment, a credential reset, or an access grant, and note which have a documented out-of-band verification step.
Determine whether staff have a defined, socially acceptable way to pause and verify a request from a senior figure, or whether declining would feel like insubordination.
Check whether approval thresholds require a second, independent person for high-value transactions, since dual authorisation blocks this attack even when the impersonation succeeds.
Review whether the organisation has agreed a verification word, callback number, or challenge procedure for unusual executive requests, and whether staff actually know it exists.
Establish whether previous training has covered synthetic media specifically, or only email-based phishing, since the instinctive trust in voice is what this exploits.
exploitationSteps: Obtain separate written consent from the impersonated executive before generating any synthetic media, and confirm legal review has cleared the approach in the relevant jurisdiction.
Keep the synthetic content minimal and strictly scoped to the agreed scenario — enough to test the process, never enough to be reusable as a general-purpose artefact.
Halt the scenario at the decision point: the finding is whether the target was willing to proceed, so stop before any transfer is initiated or access is actually granted.
Record which verification step, if any, the target attempted, since that determines whether the finding is a process gap or a training gap — the remediations differ entirely.
Debrief the participant promptly and supportively, making explicit that convincing synthetic media defeats trained professionals routinely and that this is a process finding, not a personal failure.
Destroy all synthetic audio, video and reference material at the end of the engagement and confirm destruction in writing to both the client and the impersonated executive.

examplePayloads.label: Reference material assessment (no synthesis)
examplePayloads.command: # Inventory public conference talks, earnings calls, podcast appearances and interviews; record total minutes of clean speech available.

examplePayloads.label: Urgency + confidentiality pretext framing
examplePayloads.command: I'm between sessions and can't email — we're closing the acquisition today and it must stay off the record until announced. I need you to action the transfer now.

examplePayloads.label: Authority + process-exception framing
examplePayloads.command: I know this skips the usual approval. I'm authorising it directly — treat this call as the approval and we'll document it afterwards.

examplePayloads.label: Verification-resistance probe
examplePayloads.command: # Observe whether the target attempts a callback; if they do, note whether they use a number from their own records or one supplied during the call.

examplePayloads.label: Dual-authorisation probe
examplePayloads.command: # Request an amount just below any known second-approver threshold, to test whether the threshold is the only control present.

examplePayloads.label: Halt point (mandatory)
examplePayloads.command: # Stop immediately once the target states an intention to proceed. Do not allow any transfer to be initiated.

variants: Multi-participant video calls where several synthetic colleagues corroborate the request, which defeats the instinct to verify with someone else on the call.
Voice-only impersonation over a phone call, which needs far less reference material and is substantially harder for a target to scrutinise than video.
Synthetic voice used to defeat voice-biometric authentication at a help desk or banking line.
Hybrid delivery where a compromised or spoofed executive email account establishes the pretext first and the synthetic call arrives as the expected follow-up confirmation.
mitigation: Require out-of-band verification for every high-value or unusual request, using a phone number already held in company records — never one supplied during the request itself.
Mandate dual authorisation above a defined threshold, so no single person can complete a payment regardless of how convincing the instruction was.
Agree a verification challenge for executive requests and ensure staff know that using it is expected and welcomed rather than an accusation.
Give staff explicit permission to pause and verify a request from any senior figure, and make clear in policy that no genuine executive will penalise them for it.
Train specifically on synthetic media, including that a familiar voice or face is no longer evidence of identity, and that urgency plus confidentiality is the signature combination.
Reduce the public availability of extended, high-quality executive audio where it serves no business purpose, treating it as attack-surface reduction rather than a communications restriction.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A cloned voice now takes seconds of source audio, which any executive's public speaking provides. The instinctive check people rely on — I recognise this person — no longer proves anything, and it is the check most likely to be used in exactly the high-pressure payment or access request where it matters. There have been confirmed multi-million-pound losses from this. Because you cannot train people to detect a good clone, the answer is to remove recognition from the process entirely: consequential requests are confirmed through a separate agreed channel or a shared phrase held outside the call, and no approval is ever completed on a video or voice call alone. Tell staff plainly that hearing the right voice is no longer evidence.

tools: Publicly available voice-synthesis tooling (authorised use only)
Call-recording infrastructure for evidence, where legally permitted
links: FBI IC3 advisories on business email compromise and synthetic media

items.title: Callback Phishing (Telephone-Oriented Attack Delivery)
items.prerequisites: Written authorisation naming callback phishing specifically, since staff will speak to a tester who is impersonating a third party. An agreed phone number under tester control and a script reviewed with the client in advance. Agreement on what happens if a staff member attempts to install software, and a documented stop condition. Target email addresses supplied or agreed by the client.
items.whatItIs: The email carries no link and no attachment worth scanning: it is a plain notice that a subscription has renewed and a number to call to cancel. That shape passes most mail filtering because there is nothing malicious in the message itself. The attack happens on the phone, where the tester talks the recipient into installing a remote support tool. The victim initiates the call, which makes them far more trusting than an unsolicited approach would.
items.rootCause: Mail security is built around links and attachments, so a message whose only payload is a phone number has nothing to detect. Awareness training teaches people not to click, and says much less about what to do when they dial a number themselves. The billing pretext supplies urgency and a plausible reason to act quickly, and because the recipient placed the call they treat the person answering as the legitimate party rather than a stranger.
items.impact: A successful call ends with a remote access tool installed on a corporate endpoint by the user, with their consent, from a session they started. That bypasses the controls aimed at unsolicited access and often bypasses application allowlisting too, because commercial support tools are frequently permitted. From there the attacker has interactive access as that user. Finance staff are commonly targeted because the same call can also move directly to a payment instruction.
stepsToIdentify: Establish whether mail filtering inspects message bodies for phone numbers and billing-notice patterns, or only links and attachments.
Review awareness training content for any coverage of user-initiated calls, as distinct from clicking links.
Determine which remote support tools are permitted on endpoints, and whether unapproved ones can be installed by a standard user.
Check whether the service desk has a procedure for a user reporting that they called a number from an email.
Assess whether outbound calls to unknown numbers are logged or monitored in any way.
Identify which teams handle invoices and renewals, since those roles receive billing notices routinely and are the natural targets.
exploitationSteps: Agree the pretext, the sending domain and the callback number with the client, and confirm the stop condition in writing.
Send a plain-text renewal notice with no link or attachment, containing only the callback number and an amount large enough to prompt a call.
Record how many recipients call, and how quickly, as the primary metric — this measures the part training does not cover.
Answer in character and follow the agreed script, establishing rapport before making any request.
Ask the caller to visit a support page and install the agreed tool, and record the point at which they either comply or stop.
Stop at proof of installation capability rather than establishing access, and end the call by disclosing the exercise as agreed.

examplePayloads.label: Renewal notice body
examplePayloads.command: Your annual subscription has auto-renewed at 489.00. To cancel and request a refund, call +1-555-0100 within 24 hours quoting reference 88-4417.

examplePayloads.label: Invoice-attachment variant
examplePayloads.command: # a benign PDF invoice whose only actionable content is the support number, so attachment scanning finds nothing

examplePayloads.label: Script opener
examplePayloads.command: Billing support, this is Alex. I can see the charge on your account — can you confirm the reference from the email?

examplePayloads.label: Escalation to remote tool
examplePayloads.command: The refund form needs to run on your machine. Go to support.example.test and enter the session code I give you.

examplePayloads.label: Urgency reinforcement
examplePayloads.command: The refund window closes at end of day, after that it has to go through your finance team as a dispute.

examplePayloads.label: Measurement marker
examplePayloads.command: # unique reference per recipient so each call can be attributed to a specific target

variants: A fake antivirus or security-alert pretext rather than a billing one, aimed at IT-adjacent staff.
A two-stage approach where the first call only verifies the number is live and a second call delivers the request.
Targeting accounts payable with a pretext that ends in a payment redirection instead of software installation.
A hybrid where the caller sends a follow-up email mid-call from a lookalike domain, borrowing credibility from the live conversation.
mitigation: Extend mail filtering to flag unsolicited billing notices containing phone numbers, particularly from domains with no prior correspondence.
Cover user-initiated calls explicitly in awareness training, with the specific rule that support tools are never installed during an inbound-initiated call.
Restrict installation of remote access tools to administrators, and alert on any new remote support agent appearing on an endpoint.
Give staff a single internal number to verify any unexpected billing contact, and make using it the expected behaviour rather than an exception.
Add a service desk procedure for calls of this shape, so a reporting user reaches a trained responder quickly.
Verify renewal and invoice claims against the vendor record rather than against contact details supplied in the message.
items.mitigationClientFacing: This attack sends an email with no link and no attachment — just a notice about a subscription renewal and a phone number to call. That shape passes straight through email filtering because there is nothing in it to detect, and the victim initiates the call themselves, which makes them far more trusting of whoever answers. The operator then talks them into installing remote-access software. Since your email controls cannot see this, staff guidance has to carry it: never call a number supplied in an unexpected message, look the organisation up independently, and treat any request to install software during a support call as a stop signal. Make sure your service desk knows this pattern, because staff will call them for a second opinion.

tools: A controlled VoIP number and call recording
GoPhish or an equivalent campaign platform for delivery metrics
Endpoint telemetry for detecting remote-tool installation
links: MITRE ATT&CK T1566.004: Phishing - Spearphishing Voice
CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames
NIST SP 800-115 - Technical Guide to Information Security Testing

items.title: Malicious OAuth Application Consent Phishing
items.prerequisites: A tenant using an identity provider that supports third-party application consent, such as a major cloud productivity suite. Authorisation to register an application in a tester-controlled tenant and direct staff to its consent screen. Agreement on which scopes may be requested and confirmation that no data will actually be retrieved. Visibility of the tenant's consent policy and existing application grants.
items.whatItIs: The victim is not asked for a password. They are asked to approve an application, on a genuine identity provider page, over a valid certificate, at the real domain. Everything about the page is legitimate except the application behind it. Approval issues a token to the attacker with whatever scopes were requested. Because no credential is entered, the usual signals of a phishing page are absent, and multi-factor authentication provides no protection since the user authenticated correctly.
items.rootCause: Many tenants permit users to consent to third-party applications without administrator review, a default that exists to reduce friction. Consent screens present scope names that are technically accurate but rarely meaningful to a non-specialist, so the difference between reading a profile and reading all mail is easy to miss. Tokens granted this way persist independently of the user's password, so a reset does not revoke them.
items.impact: A granted token provides ongoing programmatic access to whatever the scopes cover: mailbox contents, files, calendars, or the ability to send as the user. It survives password changes and is unaffected by MFA, so the usual containment steps do not remove it. Because access arrives through a sanctioned API path with a valid token, it looks like normal application traffic. A single approval in a finance or executive mailbox is often enough for a subsequent fraud campaign.
stepsToIdentify: Review the tenant's user consent policy: whether users may consent to any application, only to verified publishers, or not at all.
Enumerate existing application grants and note any with broad scopes, unfamiliar publishers, or consent granted by many users.
Determine whether administrator consent requests are reviewed by a named role, and how quickly.
Check whether the tenant restricts consent by publisher verification status or by application age.
Assess whether token grants are monitored, and whether an alert exists for a new application receiving mail or file scopes.
Confirm whether the incident response runbook includes revoking application grants, not just resetting passwords.
exploitationSteps: Confirm in writing which scopes may be requested and that the application will log the grant without retrieving data.
Register an application in a tester-controlled tenant with a name resembling an internal tool, and configure a redirect to a controlled endpoint.
Request the narrowest scope that still demonstrates impact, and agree that broader scopes will be discussed rather than tested.
Deliver the consent link through a pretext consistent with the named tool, such as a document-access request.
Record how many users reach the consent screen and how many approve, which separates delivery success from decision failure.
Log receipt of the token to prove the grant, then revoke it immediately and confirm with the client that it is gone.

examplePayloads.label: Consent link
examplePayloads.command: https://login.<provider>.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/authorize?client_id=<tester-app>&response_type=code&scope=Mail.Read&redirect_uri=https://listener.example.test/cb

examplePayloads.label: Pretext message
examplePayloads.command: The quarterly reporting add-in needs re-authorisation after the tenant migration. Approve access here to keep your dashboards working.

examplePayloads.label: Application naming
examplePayloads.command: # register the app with a name matching an internal convention so the consent screen reads as familiar

examplePayloads.label: Scope comparison
examplePayloads.command: # compare how the consent screen renders a narrow scope against a broad one, to document what the user is actually shown

examplePayloads.label: Token receipt marker
examplePayloads.command: # log only the token's presence, scope and expiry — never exchange it for data during the exercise

examplePayloads.label: Persistence check
examplePayloads.command: # after an agreed password reset, confirm with the client whether the grant is still active

variants: Device code phishing, where the victim is asked to enter a code on a genuine sign-in page rather than approve an application.
Abuse of an already-approved application whose credentials or redirect configuration can be influenced.
Consent requested from an administrator rather than a user, yielding tenant-wide rather than per-user scopes.
A legitimate-looking application that requests narrow scopes initially and requests incremental consent later.
mitigation: Disable unrestricted user consent, or restrict it to verified publishers and a curated set of low-risk scopes.
Route all other consent through an administrator review with a named owner and a response target.
Alert on any new application receiving mail, file or send-as scopes, and treat broad first-time grants as an incident until triaged.
Review existing grants periodically and revoke applications with no current business owner.
Add grant revocation to the account compromise runbook, since resetting a password does not invalidate an issued token.
Train staff on the specific shape of a consent screen, framing the decision as granting an application standing access rather than logging in.
items.mitigationClientFacing: In this attack nobody is asked for a password. The victim is shown a genuine sign-in page on your real identity provider, over a valid certificate, and is asked to approve an application. Everything they were taught to check is correct, so the usual advice does not help — and because no password is involved, changing passwords afterwards does not revoke the access. It persists until the approval is removed. The control is administrative: restrict who may approve third-party applications, require an administrator to review requests, and audit what has already been approved, since existing grants may predate this assessment. Reviewing that list is worth doing before anything else in this section.

reference.standard: OWASP Top 10 - A01 Broken Access Control

Tenant audit logs for consent and token events

items.title: Fake Single Sign-On Window Phishing (Browser-in-the-Browser)
items.prerequisites: Staff who authenticate to third-party services through a single sign-on popup, which is the common pattern for federated login. Authorisation to host a lookalike page on a tester-controlled domain and to collect submitted credentials under an agreed handling procedure. Agreement on credential handling, including that captured values are hashed or discarded rather than used.
items.whatItIs: Users are taught to check the address bar, so the attack renders an address bar. The page draws a convincing replica of a browser popup, complete with a padlock and the identity provider's real URL as text inside the page. The window is HTML, so every visual cue it shows is attacker-controlled. The check most users have been trained to perform is the exact check this defeats, which is what makes it more effective than an ordinary lookalike page.
items.rootCause: Awareness training reduces a complex trust decision to one heuristic: look at the URL. That heuristic assumes the address bar is chrome the page cannot draw, which stops being true once the popup is simulated in the document. Federated login has also normalised the experience of a small authentication window appearing over an unrelated site, so the pattern itself raises no suspicion. The real popup and the fake one look the same to a user who is not inspecting the DOM.
items.impact: Credentials are captured at a point where the user has no reliable way to detect the deception. Combined with a relay to the real provider, the same flow captures the session token after multi-factor authentication completes, so MFA does not stop it. The credentials are usually reusable across every service behind the same identity provider, which turns one submission into broad access. Detection is poor because the victim's experience is indistinguishable from a normal login.
stepsToIdentify: Identify which services staff reach through a federated sign-on popup, since those flows are what the attack imitates.
Determine whether the organisation uses phishing-resistant authentication anywhere, and which populations are still on password plus push or code.
Check whether conditional access requires a managed or compliant device, which would blunt a stolen credential.
Assess whether lookalike domain registration is monitored, and how quickly a newly registered similar domain would be noticed.
Review whether password managers are deployed, since a manager will not autofill on the wrong origin and gives users a reliable signal.
Establish whether sign-ins from unfamiliar infrastructure trigger any alert or step-up challenge.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, the permitted domain, and the agreed handling of any captured credentials before building anything.
Register a plausible domain and host a page whose pretext requires signing in, such as a shared document.
Render the simulated popup with the provider's real URL shown as text inside the page, matching the provider's current styling.
Deliver to the agreed recipients and record how many reach the page versus how many submit, since those measure different failures.
If session capture is in scope, relay the submission to the real provider so the user completes a genuine login and the exercise captures the resulting token.
Discard or hash credentials immediately per the agreed procedure, and report counts rather than values.

examplePayloads.command: 🔒 login..com

examplePayloads.label: Pretext landing page
examplePayloads.command: A document has been shared with you. Sign in with your work account to view it.

examplePayloads.label: Provider styling
examplePayloads.command: # mirror the provider's current sign-in CSS so the simulated window matches what users see daily

examplePayloads.label: Relay for session capture
examplePayloads.command: # forward the submission to the real provider and retain the resulting session cookie to demonstrate MFA does not prevent this

examplePayloads.label: Password-manager check
examplePayloads.command: # note whether deployed password managers decline to autofill, which is the one reliable user-facing signal

examplePayloads.label: Safe handling
examplePayloads.command: # store only a salted hash and a timestamp per submission; never retain plaintext

variants: A full adversary-in-the-middle proxy that relays the entire authentication flow rather than only the credential submission.
A device code flow where no fake page is needed at all, because the user authenticates on the genuine provider page.
Consent phishing as the follow-on step, using the captured session to approve an application for persistence.
Targeting a third-party SaaS provider's federated login rather than the primary identity provider, where monitoring is usually weaker.
mitigation: Deploy phishing-resistant authentication bound to the origin, which fails to produce a credential on a lookalike domain regardless of how convincing it looks.
Require a managed or compliant device for access to sensitive applications, so a captured credential alone is insufficient.
Deploy password managers organisation-wide and teach the autofill-refusal signal, which is more reliable than visual inspection.
Monitor for newly registered lookalike domains and have a takedown path ready before one is needed.
Alert on sign-ins from hosting-provider address space, which is where phishing relays typically run.
Update training to state plainly that a rendered address bar inside a page proves nothing, rather than reinforcing URL inspection alone.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Staff are taught to check the address bar, so this attack draws one. The page renders a convincing replica of a sign-in popup, padlock and address included, entirely inside the attacker's own page. Every visual check a user has been trained to perform gives the right answer. Since user vigilance cannot resolve this, the defences must not depend on it: password managers will not auto-fill on the wrong domain, which is a reliable signal users can be taught to trust, and hardware security keys or passkeys will not authenticate to a look-alike domain at all. Deploying a password manager broadly and phishing-resistant authentication for sensitive accounts closes this, where further training will not.

items.title: Typosquatted Domain and Watering Hole Targeting of Staff
items.prerequisites: Knowledge of the organisation's primary domains and the third-party sites its staff use routinely, which can be established through open sources and with client input. Authorisation to register lookalike domains and host content on them. Agreement on whether any payload beyond a beacon may be served, and a plan for transferring or retiring registered domains at the end of the engagement.
items.whatItIs: This tests whether the organisation would notice a lookalike domain before its staff visited one. Registration is cheap, certificates are free and automatic, so the barrier is close to zero. The variations that matter are the ones a person reading quickly will not catch: a doubled letter, a transposition, a different top-level domain, or a hyphen in a plausible place. The related watering hole case targets a third-party site staff already trust rather than imitating the organisation at all.
items.rootCause: Nothing prevents registering a similar name, and most organisations register only their exact brand plus a few obvious variants. Certificate issuance is automated and unauthenticated as to intent, so a lookalike gets the same padlock as the real site. Staff recognise the shape of a familiar domain rather than reading it character by character, which is the behaviour the attack relies on. Third-party sites staff visit daily sit outside the organisation's control entirely.
items.impact: A lookalike domain supports credential phishing, invoice fraud and malware delivery, and lends credibility to every other pretext because the sender address looks right. Where the organisation's own brand is imitated, customers and partners can be targeted too, which extends the damage beyond the organisation's own staff. A watering hole compromise reaches employees through a site the organisation never approved or monitored, so no internal control is positioned to catch it.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the organisation's domains and generate the realistic variation set: transpositions, omissions, doubled characters, homoglyphs and alternative top-level domains.
Check which variations are already registered and by whom, separating defensive registrations from third parties.
Review certificate transparency logs for newly issued certificates on names resembling the organisation's.
Establish whether any monitoring exists for lookalike registrations, and who would receive the alert.
Identify third-party sites staff use routinely, since those are the watering hole candidates.
Determine whether web filtering blocks newly registered domains as a category, which is a strong generic control here.
exploitationSteps: Agree the specific domains to register, the content to be served, and the end-of-engagement disposition in writing.
Register one or two of the most convincing variations and obtain certificates, recording how long the whole process takes.
Host a benign page that records visits, with no credential collection unless that is separately agreed.
Send an internal-looking message referencing the lookalike domain to the agreed recipients.
Record visits, and separately record whether any monitoring or filtering control reacted at any point.
Report the elapsed time from registration to first visit, since that interval is the practical detection window.

examplePayloads.command: dnstwist --registered --format csv client-domain.test

examplePayloads.label: Certificate transparency search
examplePayloads.command: # query CT logs for recently issued certificates matching the organisation's name patterns

examplePayloads.label: Plausible variation set
examplePayloads.command: exarnple.com   example-hr.com   exampIe.com   example.co

examplePayloads.label: Benign beacon page
examplePayloads.command: # static page logging timestamp, user agent and source network, with no input fields

examplePayloads.label: Internal-looking referral
examplePayloads.command: Payroll has moved to the new portal — please confirm your details at https://example-hr.com/portal before Friday.

examplePayloads.label: Detection window measurement
examplePayloads.command: # log registration time, certificate issuance time and first visit; report the gaps

variants: Homoglyph domains using visually identical characters from other scripts, which survive careful reading.
Subdomain deception where the real brand appears as a label under an attacker-controlled domain.
Compromise of a genuine third-party site staff visit, requiring no lookalike registration at all.
Lookalike registration aimed at customers or suppliers rather than employees, extending the impact outside the organisation.
mitigation: Register the highest-risk variations defensively and monitor certificate transparency logs for new issuance on similar names.
Subscribe to a brand monitoring service with an owned alert path and a pre-agreed takedown procedure.
Block newly registered domains as a web filtering category, which catches most of this class without naming individual domains.
Apply strict DMARC enforcement on owned domains so lookalikes cannot be combined with spoofing of the real one.
Tell staff that the padlock indicates encryption and not identity, since that misunderstanding is what the lookalike exploits.
Maintain an inventory of third-party sites staff depend on, and monitor those for compromise as part of supplier risk.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Domains that closely resemble yours can be registered by anyone for a few pounds, with a valid certificate issued automatically within minutes. Those domains are used to send convincing email to your staff and customers and to host sign-in pages that look correct in every visible respect. This sits outside your network, so your internal monitoring will not see it. The practical measures are to watch for newly registered look-alikes of your name and brands so you learn about one before your staff do, register the most obvious variations yourself pre-emptively, and have a takedown route ready in advance. Speed matters far more than prevention here, because registration cannot be stopped — only detected early.

tools: A registered test domain and static hosting

items.title: Mobile Number Takeover (SIM Swap) Against Staff Authentication
items.prerequisites: An organisation where any account recovery or second factor depends on SMS or voice calls to a mobile number. This case is normally assessed through review and controlled simulation rather than by attempting a real port, because an actual swap involves a third-party carrier and a real person's service. Client agreement on scope is essential, and any live element requires the consent of the individual whose number is involved.
items.whatItIs: The weak point sits at the mobile carrier, outside the organisation's control entirely. An attacker persuades carrier support to move a number to a new SIM using personal details gathered beforehand. Once the number moves, every SMS code and voice callback for that number reaches the attacker. Nothing in the organisation's environment is exploited, so no internal control is positioned to prevent it and most are not positioned to detect it either.
items.rootCause: SMS was adopted as a second factor because it was available, not because the number is securely bound to a person. Carrier verification typically relies on the same personal details that appear in data breaches and on social media. The organisation cannot see or influence the carrier's process, yet inherits its failures directly. Where SMS is also permitted as an account recovery path, it becomes a single factor rather than a second one.
items.impact: Control of the number defeats SMS-based authentication and, more seriously, SMS-based recovery, which often resets a password outright. Executives and finance staff are the usual targets because their accounts have the most value and their personal details are the most exposed. Because the compromise happens at the carrier, the organisation's first indication is typically the successful login itself, and the affected employee loses phone service at the same moment, which delays reporting.
stepsToIdentify: Inventory every place a phone number is accepted as a second factor or as an account recovery method, including third-party SaaS.
Determine whether SMS can be used to reset a password without any other factor, which is the more serious of the two exposures.
Identify which roles are both high value and publicly identifiable, since those are the realistic targets.
Assess how much personal information about those individuals is available through open sources, as that is what carrier verification will be tested against.
Check whether the organisation has guided staff to set a carrier-level port freeze or PIN on their mobile accounts.
Review whether a sudden authentication pattern change, or a help desk call reporting lost service, triggers any response.
exploitationSteps: Confirm with the client that no real port will be attempted, and agree what may be simulated instead.
Perform open-source collection against agreed individuals and record which carrier verification details are obtainable.
Map those details against the published verification requirements of the relevant carriers to assess feasibility.
Demonstrate the downstream impact using a tester-controlled account and number: show that possession of the number alone completes recovery.
Test the organisation's response by having a tester report sudden loss of mobile service to the help desk and recording what happens.
Report exposure per individual rather than in aggregate, since the risk is concentrated in a small number of people.

examplePayloads.command: # date of birth, address history, employer, partial account identifiers — the fields carriers typically verify against

examplePayloads.label: Recovery path enumeration
examplePayloads.command: # for each critical application, list every recovery method and note which need only the phone number

examplePayloads.label: Controlled recovery demonstration
examplePayloads.command: # using a tester account and tester number, complete an SMS-only password reset end to end

examplePayloads.label: Help desk probe
examplePayloads.command: My phone has no service since this morning and I cannot get my login code — can you help me in another way?

examplePayloads.label: Carrier control check
examplePayloads.command: # confirm whether each relevant carrier offers a port freeze or account PIN, and whether staff were told to enable it

examplePayloads.label: Per-individual exposure record
examplePayloads.command: # record which verification fields were obtainable for each named individual, without storing the values

variants: Port-out fraud, moving the number to a different carrier rather than swapping the SIM at the current one.
An eSIM profile transfer, which can be faster and leaves a different trail than a physical swap.
Compromise of a voicemail system where codes are delivered by voice call and retrieved from the mailbox.
Targeting a personal email account that serves as the recovery path for a corporate one.
mitigation: Remove SMS and voice from account recovery entirely, which is the more urgent of the two changes.
Move second-factor authentication to phishing-resistant methods, or at minimum to an authenticator application rather than SMS.
Advise high-risk staff to set a carrier port freeze or account PIN, and verify adoption rather than assuming it.
Alert on second-factor method changes and on authentication from a new device shortly after such a change.
Give the help desk a procedure for a reported loss of mobile service that treats it as a potential compromise rather than a connectivity issue.
Reduce the public exposure of high-risk staff's personal details where the organisation has any influence over it.
items.mitigationClientFacing: For any account where a second factor is delivered by text message, the real control sits with your employees' mobile carriers rather than with you. An attacker who persuades carrier support to move a number to a new SIM receives those codes, and the employee simply loses signal — often at night, when nobody investigates for hours. You cannot fix the carrier's process. What you can do is stop depending on it: move second-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app or, better, a hardware key, starting with administrators, finance and executives. Ask staff in those roles to add a port-out PIN with their carrier, and treat an employee's unexplained loss of mobile service as a security event.

reference.standard: NIST SP 800-63B - Authentication and Lifecycle Management
tools: Tester-controlled account and number for the controlled demonstration

CWE-304: Missing Critical Step in Authentication

items.title: Collaboration Platform Phishing via External Federation
items.prerequisites: An organisation using a chat or collaboration platform with external access enabled: federated messaging, guest accounts, or shared channels with partner organisations. A tester-controlled tenant on the same platform, or a guest account the client provisions. Agreement on which staff may be contacted and what may be sent, since messages arrive in a space staff treat as internal.
items.whatItIs: Every control the organisation built for email sits on the email path. A message arriving in the chat client passes none of it: no gateway, no attachment detonation, no external-sender banner in most default configurations. Staff have spent years learning to be careful with email and have no equivalent instinct for a chat message, because chat has historically meant colleagues. Federation quietly changed that without changing the perception.
items.rootCause: External access is frequently enabled by default or turned on for one partner and never scoped back. The platform's own warnings about external participants are subtle and easy to miss once a conversation is underway. Security investment has concentrated on email because that is where attacks historically arrived, leaving the chat path with substantially less inspection. The trust users place in the channel is inherited from when it genuinely was internal only.
items.impact: A link or file delivered in chat reaches the user with less inspection and more trust than the same content in email. Attachments may bypass detonation entirely depending on configuration. The conversational format also supports pretexting far better than email does, because the attacker can answer questions in real time and adapt. Where the platform integrates with file storage, a shared file can carry a credential-harvesting link that appears to originate inside the organisation's own environment.
stepsToIdentify: Determine which external access modes are enabled: open federation, allowlisted domains, guest accounts, or shared channels.
Establish whether external contact is restricted to named partner domains or permitted from any tenant.
Check whether files shared through chat pass through the same inspection as email attachments.
Assess how clearly the client marks external participants, and whether that marking persists throughout a conversation.
Review whether chat messages are retained and searchable for incident response to the same standard as mail.
Confirm whether staff have any reporting mechanism for a suspicious chat message equivalent to the report-phish button in mail.
exploitationSteps: Agree scope, the tester tenant identity, and the specific staff who may be contacted.
Initiate contact from the tester tenant and record whether the message is delivered, blocked, or flagged.
Note precisely how the external warning is presented, and whether it remains visible after the first exchange.
Establish a pretext through a short conversational exchange rather than a single message, since dialogue is the advantage this channel provides.
Send a benign tracked link and, separately, a benign file, to compare inspection on each path.
Record the response rate and the reporting rate, since the difference from the organisation's email baseline is the finding.

examplePayloads.label: Opening message
examplePayloads.command: Hi — I'm covering the vendor onboarding from our side. Are you the right contact for the supplier portal access?

examplePayloads.label: Tracked link
examplePayloads.command: Here's the onboarding checklist: https://listener.example.test/onboarding

examplePayloads.label: Benign file inspection test
examplePayloads.command: # send a harmless test file and compare whether it is inspected the way an email attachment would be

examplePayloads.label: External-warning capture
examplePayloads.command: # screenshot the external-participant indicator at first contact and again after three exchanges

examplePayloads.label: Support impersonation
examplePayloads.command: IT service desk here — we're validating the new sign-in for your account, can you confirm the code you just received?

examplePayloads.label: Reporting-path check
examplePayloads.command: # note whether the client offers any way to report the message, and where it goes

variants: A compromised partner tenant, where the messages genuinely originate from a federated organisation the target trusts.
A malicious application or bot installed into a workspace, messaging users with the platform's own credibility.
Guest account abuse in a shared channel, where the attacker is a legitimate channel member.
Voice or video call pretexting through the same platform, which carries even more implied trust than text.
mitigation: Restrict external access to an allowlist of partner domains rather than open federation, and review the list periodically.
Route files and links shared through chat via the same inspection pipeline used for email.
Configure prominent, persistent external-participant warnings rather than relying on a first-message indicator.
Provide a reporting action in the chat client and route it to the same queue as reported phishing mail.
Include chat-delivered pretexting in awareness training, since staff extend email caution to chat only when told to.
Retain and monitor chat messages for incident response to the same standard as email, including external conversations.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Every control you built for phishing sits on the email path. A message arriving in your chat platform from an external organisation passes none of it — no gateway, no attachment scanning, no warning banner — and lands in a tool staff treat as internal and therefore trusted. This is a real and growing gap. Restrict which external organisations may message your staff directly, so the default is closed rather than open; make external senders visibly marked in the interface; and extend link and file scanning to the chat platform as you have for email. Tell staff explicitly that a message in the chat tool is not inherently more trustworthy than an email, because most people assume otherwise.

A controlled HTTP listener for link tracking
Platform external access and federation configuration review

items.title: Insider Recruitment and Bribery Approach Susceptibility
items.prerequisites: Explicit written authorisation from executive sponsorship and, in most jurisdictions, from legal counsel, since this involves approaching named employees with an offer. Agreement on which individuals may be approached, the exact wording of any offer, and an immediate stop condition. This case is frequently assessed as a control review rather than a live approach, and that choice should be made with the client before anything is sent.
items.whatItIs: This examines whether an employee approached with an offer would report it, and whether the organisation would notice if they did not. Approaches are real and increasingly direct: a message offering payment for access, credentials or a click. Unlike phishing, there is no deception about what is being asked, so the defence is entirely cultural and procedural rather than technical. What is being measured is the reporting rate and the organisation's ability to detect misuse if reporting fails.
items.rootCause: Most organisations have no reporting path for this specific situation and no stated expectation that an approach should be reported. Staff who receive one often stay silent out of embarrassment or fear of being suspected. Monitoring is typically designed to detect intrusion rather than authorised access being used improperly, so an employee acting within their normal permissions produces no alert. Financial pressure and grievance, the usual motivators, are not visible to security teams at all.
items.impact: A cooperating insider starts inside every perimeter control, with legitimate credentials and a legitimate reason to be in the systems they touch. Detection depends entirely on behavioural monitoring and separation of duties, which are often the weakest controls present. The damage ranges from a single deliberate click that establishes a foothold to sustained data exfiltration over months. Because activity looks authorised, discovery is usually late and reconstructing what happened is difficult.
stepsToIdentify: Establish whether any policy or training addresses being approached with an offer, as distinct from insider threat monitoring.
Determine whether a confidential reporting channel exists, whether staff know about it, and whether it can be used anonymously.
Identify which roles could cause the most damage with their existing access, since those are where an approach would be aimed.
Assess what monitoring would detect misuse of legitimate access: volume alerts, unusual access patterns, or separation of duties on high-value actions.
Review joiner, mover and leaver processes, since accumulated access from previous roles increases what any individual could do.
Check whether the organisation has ever received such a report, and what happened, which indicates whether the path works in practice.
exploitationSteps: Confirm executive and legal authorisation in writing, naming the individuals and the exact message wording.
Prefer a control review over a live approach unless the client specifically wants the reporting rate measured.
If approaching, use the agreed wording and send to the agreed individuals only, with no follow-up beyond the first message.
Measure the reporting rate and the time to report, which are the outcomes that matter here.
Stop immediately at any indication of interest and escalate to the named client contact rather than continuing the exchange.
Debrief every approached individual promptly, regardless of how they responded, and make clear the exercise was authorised.

examplePayloads.label: Direct approach
examplePayloads.command: We pay for access. If you can run a file on your work machine, there's a four-figure payment in it. Interested?

examplePayloads.label: Gradual approach
examplePayloads.command: I work in competitive research and pay for industry insight. Would you be open to an informal paid conversation?

examplePayloads.label: Grievance framing
examplePayloads.command: # an approach referencing a publicly visible restructure or dispute, which is the usual real-world hook

examplePayloads.label: Reporting-path test
examplePayloads.command: # after the approach, measure how many recipients used the confidential channel and how long it took

examplePayloads.label: Control review substitute
examplePayloads.command: # where no live approach is authorised, review policy, training, reporting channel and detection capability instead

examplePayloads.label: Detection capability probe
examplePayloads.command: # with client agreement, have an authorised user access an unusual volume of records and check whether anything alerts

variants: Recruitment through a hiring pretext, where a fake role interview is used to elicit internal detail rather than to buy access.
Approaches to contractors or outsourced staff, who often hold comparable access with weaker vetting and less loyalty.
Coercion rather than payment, using personal information obtained beforehand as leverage.
Targeting a departing employee during a notice period, when access frequently remains intact and motivation may have changed.
mitigation: State clearly in policy and training that approaches happen, are not the employee's fault, and must be reported.
Provide a confidential reporting channel that permits anonymity, and publicise it repeatedly rather than once at induction.
Apply least privilege and separation of duties on the actions that would cause the most damage, so no one individual suffices.
Monitor for misuse of legitimate access, including volume anomalies and access outside a role's normal pattern.
Review access on role change rather than only on departure, since accumulated permissions are what make an insider valuable.
Treat a reported approach as a positive outcome and respond supportively, because the reporting rate depends on how the first report was handled.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Employees are approached with offers of payment for access, and these approaches are real rather than theoretical — they arrive through professional networks, messaging apps and recruitment contacts. This assessment looked at two things: whether someone approached would report it, and whether you would notice if they did not. Both matter, and the first is largely a question of whether reporting feels safe. Provide a confidential route that does not go through the employee's own line manager, say plainly that reporting an approach is welcomed rather than treated with suspicion, and make sure people know the route exists before they need it. Alongside that, ensure sensitive actions leave records that someone other than the person performing them reviews.

items.title: No Logging or Review of Physical Badge Access
items.prerequisites: Access to review the badge/physical-access system and its logs (or evidence of their absence), and authorization for the review. Coordination with facilities.
items.whatItIs: Badge systems record who entered which door and when — invaluable for detecting tailgating, after-hours access, and misuse. If those logs are not kept, or are kept but never reviewed, physical access goes unaccountable. This assessment checks whether physical access events are logged and reviewed.
items.rootCause: Badge logs are treated as an operational feature, not a security record, so review is nobody's job. Some systems retain little history, and no one correlates access with expected patterns.
items.impact: Without reviewed access logs, an intruder's tailgating, a terminated employee's continued access, or after-hours misuse goes unnoticed, and investigations lack a record of who was physically present.
items.realWorldContext: After physical security incidents, organizations frequently discover their badge logs either weren't retained or were never reviewed — so no one noticed the after-hours access or the shared badge until it was far too late. Reviewing physical access is basic accountability that is routinely skipped.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether the badge/access system logs entry events with identity and timestamp.
Check log retention and whether logs are centralized.
Assess whether anyone reviews access logs or receives alerts.
Look for detection of tailgating, after-hours, or anomalous access.
Check whether terminated staff badges are promptly revoked and would show in logs.
Document the logging and review gaps.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to review the physical-access system with facilities.
Examine badge logs for completeness (identity, door, timestamp) and retention.
Assess whether reviews or alerts occur for anomalous access.
Test (in scope) whether an after-hours or unusual access would be noticed.
Check revocation of a departed-staff badge against the logs.
Document the accountability gap.

examplePayloads.label: Review access-log completeness
examplePayloads.command: # examine sample badge events for identity, door, and timestamp fields

examplePayloads.label: Check retention window
examplePayloads.command: # how far back does the badge system retain access events?

examplePayloads.label: Test after-hours access visibility (in scope)
examplePayloads.command: # with authorization, perform a benign after-hours badge-in and check for any review/alert

examplePayloads.label: Verify revocation shows in logs
examplePayloads.command: # confirm a revoked badge is denied and the denial is logged

variants: No badge logging at all (open or mechanical access).
Logs retained but never reviewed.
No alerting on after-hours or anomalous access.
Terminated staff badges still active and unreviewed.
mitigation: Log all physical access events with identity and timestamp, centrally retained.
Review access logs regularly and alert on anomalies (after-hours, tailgating patterns).
Promptly revoke access for departed staff and audit revocations.
Correlate physical access with other security events.
Retain logs long enough to support investigations.
Assign clear ownership for access-log review.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your badge system can record who came in which door and when, which helps catch intruders, after-hours misuse, or ex-employees still getting in — but only if those records are kept and someone reviews them. The fix is to log all door access with identity and time, review it regularly with alerts for unusual access, and promptly cancel badges when people leave.

reference.standard: AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting)

items.title: Visitor Logs Not Kept or Reviewed
items.prerequisites: Ability to observe the visitor sign-in process and review visitor records (or their absence), and authorization to do so. A visit as a pretext, if in scope.
items.whatItIs: A visitor log records who came in, who they visited, and when — a basic accountability control and a deterrent. If visitors are not signed in, or the log is never reviewed, there is no record of who was on the premises, aiding intruders and undermining investigations. This assessment checks visitor-logging practice.
items.rootCause: Reception is busy and visitor logging feels like a formality, so it is skipped or done inconsistently, and no one reviews it. There is no accountability for who entered as a 'visitor'.
items.impact: Without visitor logs, an intruder using a visitor pretext leaves no record, tailgating is unaccountable, and investigators cannot establish who was present. It also removes a deterrent to casual intrusion.
items.realWorldContext: Social-engineering assessors routinely walk in as 'visitors' and are never properly signed in, leaving no trace of their presence. A missing or unreviewed visitor log is both an open door and an evidence gap that real intruders exploit.
stepsToIdentify: Observe the visitor sign-in process (or its absence).
Check whether visitors are consistently logged with host, time, and purpose.
Assess whether visitor badges are issued and returned.
Determine whether visitor logs are retained and reviewed.
Where in scope, attempt entry as a visitor and see whether it is properly recorded.
Document the visitor-accountability gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization for any pretext visit and record review.
Observe or test the visitor sign-in process.
Assess consistency, badge issuance/return, and record retention.
If in scope, enter as a visitor and check whether the entry is logged accurately.
Determine whether anyone reviews visitor records.
Document the logging and review gaps.
