examplePayloads.command: # note whether every visitor is logged with host, purpose, and time

examplePayloads.label: Test visitor entry (in scope)
examplePayloads.command: # with authorization, sign in (or attempt to bypass) and verify the record created

examplePayloads.label: Check badge issuance/return
examplePayloads.command: # is a visitor badge issued, worn, and collected on exit?

examplePayloads.label: Review retention
examplePayloads.command: # are visitor records kept and ever reviewed?

variants: No visitor sign-in at all.
Inconsistent logging (some visitors unrecorded).
Visitor badges not returned/tracked.
Logs kept but never reviewed.
mitigation: Require consistent visitor sign-in with host, purpose, and time.
Issue, track, and collect visitor badges.
Retain and periodically review visitor records.
Escort visitors in sensitive areas.
Reconcile visitor logs with badge/access events.
Train reception on the security purpose of visitor logging.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A visitor log records who came in, who they were visiting, and when — it's a basic accountability measure and a deterrent. If visitors aren't signed in or the log is never checked, there's no record of who was in the building. The fix is to consistently sign in visitors with their host and purpose, issue and collect visitor badges, and keep and review the records.

items.title: Help-Desk Password-Reset Actions Not Logged or Attributable
items.prerequisites: Ability to review help-desk processes and logs (or their absence), and authorization to do so. A vishing pretext, if in scope.
items.whatItIs: The help desk can reset passwords and grant access — a powerful capability and a prime social-engineering target. If reset actions are not logged with who requested, who approved, and how identity was verified, malicious resets (via vishing) cannot be detected or attributed. This assessment checks accountability for help-desk identity actions.
items.rootCause: Help-desk tooling logs the technical action but rarely the verification performed or the requester's proven identity, and vishing exploits the pressure to be helpful. Without accountable logging, a socially-engineered reset looks like a normal one.
items.impact: An attacker who vishes the help desk into a password reset gains account access, and without accountable logging the malicious reset blends in — no record of weak verification, no way to detect or trace it.
items.realWorldContext: Help-desk vishing has driven major breaches: an attacker calls posing as an employee, pressures the agent into a reset or MFA re-enrollment, and walks into the account. When reset actions aren't logged with the verification performed, these attacks are invisible after the fact — which is exactly what makes the help desk such a favoured target.
stepsToIdentify: Review the help-desk password-reset and access-grant process.
Check whether identity-verification steps are required and logged.
Assess whether reset actions record requester, approver, and verification method.
Determine whether resets are reviewed or alerted on (especially privileged accounts).
Where in scope, test the process with a vishing pretext (coordinated).
Document the accountability and verification gaps.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization (and coordination) for any vishing test.
Review the reset process and its logging.
Assess what identity verification is required and whether it is recorded.
If in scope, attempt a socially-engineered reset and observe verification and logging.
Check whether resets on sensitive accounts trigger review/alerts.
Document the gaps and their exploitability.

examplePayloads.command: # do reset records include requester, approver, and verification method?

examplePayloads.label: Assess verification requirements
examplePayloads.command: # what identity proof is required before a reset? is it enforced and logged?

examplePayloads.label: Coordinated vishing test (in scope)
examplePayloads.command: # with authorization, call the help desk with a pretext and record verification/logging outcome

examplePayloads.label: Check sensitive-account handling
examplePayloads.command: # are resets on admin/exec accounts reviewed or alerted?

variants: Resets logged without the verification performed.
No requester identity proof recorded.
Privileged-account resets not reviewed.
MFA re-enrollment via help desk unlogged.
mitigation: Log help-desk identity actions with requester, approver, and verification method.
Require and record strong identity verification before resets.
Apply stricter verification and review for privileged accounts.
Alert on and review sensitive resets and MFA re-enrollments.
Train help-desk staff to resist social-engineering pressure.
Provide callback/verification procedures for high-risk requests.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your help desk can reset passwords and grant access, which makes it a favourite target for attackers who call pretending to be staff. If resets aren't logged with how the person's identity was checked, a fraudulent reset looks just like a real one. The fix is to require and record strong identity checks before any reset, log who requested and approved it, apply extra scrutiny to important accounts, and train staff to resist pressure.

items.title: No Audit Trail of Who Granted Physical or System Access
items.prerequisites: Access to review access-provisioning records (badge grants, account grants) or their absence, and authorization to do so.
items.whatItIs: Granting access — issuing a badge, creating an account, adding someone to a privileged group — should be recorded with who requested, who approved, and why. If those grants are not logged, inappropriate or malicious access cannot be detected or traced back. This assessment checks accountability for access-granting decisions.
items.rootCause: Provisioning is often handled informally (a verbal request, a quick ticket) without capturing approver and justification. Without an audit trail, over-granting and unauthorized grants are invisible.
items.impact: Unlogged grants let an attacker (or insider) obtain access without accountability — a badge for an area they shouldn't reach, membership in a privileged group — with no record to detect or reverse it.
items.realWorldContext: Insider-threat and social-engineering investigations frequently stall on the question 'who granted this access and why?' — because no one recorded it. An access grant without an approver and justification is an accountability black hole that both attackers and negligent insiders exploit.
stepsToIdentify: Review how physical and system access is granted and whether grants are logged.
Check whether records capture requester, approver, justification, and date.
Assess whether grants require documented approval.
Determine whether access grants are periodically reviewed/recertified.
Look for access that cannot be traced to an authorized grant.
Document the provisioning-accountability gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to review provisioning records.
Examine sample access grants for approver, justification, and date.
Identify grants with no documented approval.
Assess whether periodic access reviews/recertification occur.
Show that an untraceable grant could not be detected or reversed.
Document the accountability gap.

examplePayloads.command: # do provisioning records capture requester, approver, justification, date?

examplePayloads.label: Sample privileged-group additions
examplePayloads.command: # for a sample, trace each to an approved request

examplePayloads.label: Check recertification
examplePayloads.command: # is access periodically reviewed and re-approved?

examplePayloads.command: # identify any access with no corresponding approved grant

variants: Access granted verbally with no record.
Privileged-group additions without documented approval.
Badge grants with no approver captured.
No periodic access recertification.
mitigation: Require and log documented approval for all access grants (requester, approver, justification).
Maintain an auditable provisioning trail for physical and system access.
Perform periodic access reviews/recertification.
Alert on privileged-access grants.
Reconcile actual access against approved grants.
Assign ownership for provisioning accountability.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Whenever someone is given access — a badge, an account, a spot in an admin group — it should be recorded with who asked, who approved, and why. If that isn't logged, inappropriate access can't be spotted or traced. The fix is to require documented approval for every access grant, keep an auditable record, and periodically review who has access and re-confirm they still need it.

items.title: Security Guard Rounds and Incidents Not Recorded
items.prerequisites: Ability to review guard-tour and incident-recording practices (or their absence), and authorization to do so. Observation over time.
items.whatItIs: Where physical security relies on guards, their patrol rounds and incident observations should be recorded — proving coverage and creating a trail of what was seen. If rounds and incidents are not logged, there is no assurance patrols happen or record of anomalies, weakening physical accountability. This assessment checks guard-activity recording.
items.rootCause: Guard logging is often paper-based, inconsistent, or absent, and incidents are handled verbally. Without recorded rounds and incidents, coverage is unverifiable and observations are lost.
items.impact: Unrecorded patrols mean gaps in coverage go unnoticed and an intruder timing patrols faces less risk; unlogged incidents mean anomalies (a propped door, an unfamiliar person) are never escalated or investigated.
items.realWorldContext: Assessors observing a site often find guard patrols are irregular and unrecorded, and 'incidents' like a propped fire door are noticed but never logged or escalated. Without a record of rounds and observations, physical coverage is a matter of trust rather than evidence — a gap intruders time their entry around.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether guard patrol rounds are scheduled and recorded (guard-tour system or log).
Check whether incidents/observations are recorded and escalated.
Assess coverage: are rounds consistent, or predictable/skippable?
Determine whether records are reviewed by management.
Observe (in scope) whether an anomaly you introduce is noticed and logged.
Document the guard-accountability gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to observe and review guard practices.
Review round scheduling and recording mechanisms.
Assess incident-recording and escalation practice.
Introduce a benign, safe anomaly (e.g. a noticeable but harmless item) and see whether it is observed and logged.
Check whether records are reviewed and gaps addressed.
Document the coverage and recording gaps.

examplePayloads.command: # are patrol rounds logged (guard-tour checkpoints/timestamps)?

examplePayloads.label: Assess predictability
examplePayloads.command: # are rounds at fixed, predictable times an intruder could avoid?

examplePayloads.label: Test anomaly detection (in scope)
examplePayloads.command: # place a benign, obvious anomaly and record whether it is noticed and logged

examplePayloads.label: Check escalation
examplePayloads.command: # are observed incidents recorded and escalated to management?

variants: No recording of patrol rounds.
Predictable patrol timing enabling avoidance.
Incidents handled verbally and never logged.
Records kept but never reviewed.
mitigation: Use a guard-tour system to record patrol rounds with checkpoints and timestamps.
Randomize patrol timing to reduce predictability.
Record and escalate incidents/observations consistently.
Review guard records and address coverage gaps.
Correlate guard records with access and camera events.
Train guards on recording and escalation expectations.
items.mitigationClientFacing: If your physical security relies on guards, their patrols and anything unusual they notice should be recorded — otherwise you can't prove patrols happen or track what was seen, and an intruder can time predictable rounds. The fix is to record patrol rounds with checkpoints and times, vary the timing, log and escalate anything unusual, and review those records. Recorded patrols turn physical security from something you hope is happening into something you can prove and improve over time.

items.title: No Standardized Visitor-Management Process
items.prerequisites: Ability to observe visitor handling across entrances/sites, and authorization to do so. A pretext visit, if in scope.
items.whatItIs: A consistent, documented visitor-management process — sign-in, ID check, badge, escort rules — is a baseline physical control. When each entrance or receptionist handles visitors differently, attackers find the weakest one. This assessment checks whether visitor management is standardized and enforced as a baseline.
items.rootCause: Visitor handling grows ad hoc per site and per receptionist, with no documented standard. Inconsistency creates a weakest link an attacker can target.
items.impact: Inconsistent visitor management lets an attacker enter via the least-controlled entrance or the most accommodating receptionist, bypassing tighter controls elsewhere.
items.realWorldContext: Social-engineering assessors deliberately shop for the weakest entrance, and inconsistent visitor processes reliably provide one — a side reception with no ID check, or a stand-in receptionist who waves people through. Standardizing the process removes the soft spot attackers seek.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether a documented visitor-management standard exists.
Observe visitor handling across multiple entrances/sites/receptionists.
Identify inconsistencies (ID checks, badges, escort, sign-in) between them.
Find the weakest entry point.
Where in scope, attempt entry via the weakest point.
Document the baseline-consistency gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization for observation and any pretext entry.
Review the visitor-management standard (or its absence).
Observe handling at several entrances and note variations.
Identify the least-controlled entry.
If in scope, enter via the weakest point and document the process failure.
Document the inconsistency and its exploitability.

examplePayloads.command: # observe ID check, badge, escort, sign-in at each entrance/reception

examplePayloads.label: Identify the weakest point
examplePayloads.command: # rank entrances by control strength; pick the softest

examplePayloads.label: Test the weak entrance (in scope)
examplePayloads.command: # with authorization, attempt entry via the least-controlled reception

examplePayloads.label: Check for a documented standard
examplePayloads.command: # is there a written, enforced visitor-management process?

variants: Side entrance with no ID check.
Stand-in receptionist unaware of the process.
Some sites escort visitors, others don't.
Badge issuance inconsistent across entrances.
mitigation: Document and enforce a standard visitor-management process across all entrances/sites.
Require consistent ID checks, badges, sign-in, and escort rules.
Train all reception and stand-in staff on the standard.
Audit entrances for consistency periodically.
Remove or control weak/secondary entrances.
Provide clear procedures for exceptions.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A consistent visitor process — sign-in, ID check, badge, escort — is a basic control, but when each entrance or receptionist does it differently, attackers simply use the weakest one. The fix is to write down one visitor process, apply it at every entrance, train all reception staff (including stand-ins) on it, and check periodically that it's followed consistently. A consistent process at every entrance removes the weak spot attackers look for, and it costs nothing beyond training and attention.

items.title: Inconsistent Badge-Issuance and Access Baseline
items.prerequisites: Ability to review badge-issuance practice and access levels, and authorization to do so.
items.whatItIs: Badges and their access levels should follow a documented baseline — who gets what access, how badges are issued and photographed, and how access maps to role. When badge issuance is inconsistent and access is granted ad hoc, people accumulate access beyond their role and unauthorized badges slip through. This assessment checks the badge/access baseline.
items.rootCause: Access is granted per request without a role-based baseline, and badge issuance varies by who handles it. Over-provisioning and inconsistent issuance follow.
items.impact: Inconsistent baselines lead to excessive physical access (people reaching areas they shouldn't) and to weakly-issued badges an attacker can obtain or clone, undermining physical segmentation.
items.realWorldContext: Assessments routinely find staff with badge access to areas they have no business entering, granted ad hoc and never reviewed — and badge issuance so inconsistent that obtaining or cloning one is easy. A role-based access baseline is what keeps physical access proportionate and controllable.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether a role-based physical-access baseline exists.
Assess badge-issuance consistency (ID proof, photo, access mapping).
Sample staff access levels against their roles for over-provisioning.
Check whether access is periodically reviewed/recertified.
Assess badge technology strength (cloneable?) as part of the baseline.
Document the baseline and issuance gaps.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to review badge issuance and access levels.
Examine the issuance process and any access baseline.
Sample access grants against roles to find over-provisioning.
Assess badge technology and cloneability.
Show that inconsistent issuance or excessive access is exploitable.
Document the configuration-management gap.

examplePayloads.label: Review access-to-role mapping
examplePayloads.command: # sample staff and compare their badge access to their role

examplePayloads.label: Assess issuance consistency
examplePayloads.command: # is ID proof, photo, and access mapping required and consistent?

examplePayloads.label: Evaluate badge cloneability
examplePayloads.command: # with authorization, assess badge tech (e.g. low-frequency 125kHz cloneable with Proxmark)

examplePayloads.label: Check recertification
examplePayloads.command: # is physical access periodically reviewed against role?

variants: Staff with access far beyond their role.
Badges issued without ID proof or photo.
Cloneable low-frequency badge technology.
No periodic review of physical access.
mitigation: Define a role-based physical-access baseline and grant access to match.
Standardize badge issuance (ID proof, photo, access mapping).
Use strong, non-trivially-cloneable badge technology.
Periodically review and recertify physical access.
Alert on out-of-baseline access grants.
Audit issuance and access against the baseline.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Badges and the areas they open should follow a clear plan based on people's roles, but when access is granted ad hoc and badges are issued inconsistently, staff end up able to enter areas they shouldn't and weak badges slip through. The fix is to base access on role, standardize how badges are issued (with ID and photo), use badge technology that's hard to copy, and regularly review who can go where.

items.title: No Baseline for Information Reception May Disclose
items.prerequisites: Ability to interact with reception/front-line staff (in scope) and review any disclosure guidance. Authorization for pretext interaction.
items.whatItIs: Front-line staff (reception, help desk) field questions all day, and without a clear baseline of what they may and may not disclose, they can leak useful information — staff names and roles, whether someone is in, internal phone numbers, org structure — to a pretexting caller or visitor. This assessment checks whether information-disclosure limits are defined and followed.
items.rootCause: Reception's job is to be helpful, and without a documented disclosure baseline they answer questions naturally. Pretexting exploits this to gather reconnaissance.
items.impact: Disclosed details (names, roles, schedules, internal numbers) feed targeted phishing/vishing and pretexting, and confirm an attacker's assumptions, making later attacks far more convincing.
items.realWorldContext: Pretext callers routinely harvest an org chart, who's on holiday, and internal extensions from a helpful receptionist — reconnaissance that makes the next phishing or vishing attempt land. A defined disclosure baseline is what turns 'always helpful' into 'helpful within safe limits'.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether reception/front-line staff have disclosure guidance.
Assess what information is considered non-disclosable (schedules, structure, numbers).
Where in scope, use a pretext to probe what staff will disclose.
Identify over-disclosure that aids reconnaissance.
Check whether staff verify caller/visitor identity before disclosing.
Document the disclosure-baseline gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization for pretext interaction with staff.
Review any disclosure guidance/baseline.
Probe (via a coordinated pretext) what information staff will provide.
Record the reconnaissance obtainable through normal interaction.
Assess identity verification before disclosure.
Document the disclosure gaps and their reconnaissance value.

examplePayloads.label: Test schedule disclosure
examplePayloads.command: # ask whether a named person is in/travelling and record the response

examplePayloads.label: Assess identity verification
examplePayloads.command: # does staff verify who is asking before disclosing?

examplePayloads.label: Compare against a baseline
examplePayloads.command: # is there defined guidance on what may/may not be disclosed?

variants: Reception confirming staff presence/absence to unknown callers.
Internal extensions/org structure disclosed freely.
Executive travel schedules revealed.
No identity verification before disclosure.
mitigation: Define a disclosure baseline: what front-line staff may and may not reveal.
Require identity verification before disclosing sensitive details.
Train reception/help desk on pretexting and safe responses.
Route sensitive requests through verified channels.
Test disclosure resistance periodically.
Provide scripts for declining and verifying requests.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Reception and help-desk staff answer questions all day, and without clear limits they can unintentionally reveal useful information — who works there, who's in, internal numbers — to a scammer building an attack. The fix is to define what staff may and may not disclose, require them to verify who's asking before sharing sensitive details, and train them to recognize pretext calls.

items.title: Unmanaged Contractor Onboarding/Offboarding for Physical Access
items.prerequisites: Ability to review contractor access processes and current contractor access, and authorization to do so.
items.whatItIs: Contractors, cleaners, and temporary staff are often granted physical (and sometimes system) access with little process, and their access is frequently not revoked when they leave. Without managed onboarding/offboarding as a controlled change, orphaned access accumulates. This assessment checks contractor access lifecycle management.
items.rootCause: Contractor access is arranged quickly and informally, and offboarding is nobody's clear responsibility, so badges and accounts persist after the engagement ends.
items.impact: Orphaned contractor access — an active badge for a departed cleaner or contractor — provides an attacker (or the former contractor) an unmonitored way in, bypassing controls under a legitimate-looking identity.
items.realWorldContext: Terminated-contractor access that was never revoked is a recurring finding and a real breach vector — a former cleaner's badge still opening doors, a departed contractor's account still active. Treating contractor access as a controlled change with mandatory offboarding is what closes it.
stepsToIdentify: Review how contractor/temporary physical access is granted and revoked.
Assess whether onboarding requires approval and offboarding is mandatory and tracked.
Sample current contractor access against active engagements.
Identify orphaned access (departed contractors still active).
Check whether contractor access is time-limited/expiring.
Document the lifecycle-management gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to review contractor access.
Examine onboarding/offboarding processes and records.
Sample active contractor badges/accounts against current engagements.
Identify access that should have been revoked.
Show that orphaned access grants an unmonitored entry.
Document the change-control gap.

examplePayloads.label: Find orphaned access
examplePayloads.command: # identify access for contractors whose engagement has ended

examplePayloads.label: Check for access expiry
examplePayloads.command: # is contractor access time-limited and auto-expiring?

examplePayloads.label: Review offboarding ownership
examplePayloads.command: # who is responsible for revoking contractor access, and is it tracked?

variants: Departed cleaner's badge still active.
Contractor account not disabled after project end.
No expiry on contractor access.
No clear owner for contractor offboarding.
mitigation: Treat contractor access as a controlled change with documented approval.
Make offboarding mandatory, tracked, and owned.
Time-limit contractor access with automatic expiry.
Periodically reconcile contractor access against active engagements.
Alert on contractor access outside an engagement window.
Include contractors in access recertification.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Contractors and cleaners often get building access quickly and informally, and it's frequently never turned off when they leave — leaving active badges and accounts an attacker (or the former contractor) can use. The fix is to require approval to grant contractor access, make revoking it a mandatory tracked step when they leave, set access to expire automatically, and regularly check that current access matches current engagements.

items.title: No Clean-Desk / Sensitive-Information Handling Baseline
items.prerequisites: Ability to walk authorized areas and observe desks/printers/whiteboards, and authorization to do so. A camera.
items.whatItIs: A clean-desk and information-handling baseline defines how sensitive material (documents, credentials, whiteboards, screens) is handled and secured. Without one, passwords on sticky notes, sensitive printouts left on desks, and confidential whiteboards accumulate — easy pickings for a visitor or after-hours intruder. This assessment checks the clean-desk baseline.
items.rootCause: Convenience wins without a defined standard: people leave documents out, write passwords down, and don't clear whiteboards. There is no baseline making them treat this material as sensitive.
items.impact: Sensitive material left exposed hands an attacker credentials, internal documents, and confidential information directly, with no technical attack required, during a visit or after-hours access.
items.realWorldContext: Walking an office after hours (or as a visitor) and photographing sticky-note passwords, sensitive printouts, and un-erased whiteboards is a staple of physical assessments — it works almost everywhere without a clean-desk baseline. It is one of the highest-yield, lowest-effort findings in physical testing.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether a clean-desk / information-handling baseline exists.
Walk authorized areas and observe desks, printers, whiteboards, and screens.
Photograph exposed credentials, sensitive documents, and confidential whiteboards.
Assess printer/output handling (unclaimed sensitive prints).
Check screen-lock and privacy practices.
Document the handling-baseline gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to walk areas and photograph exposed material.
Observe and record exposed sensitive material.
Assess the range of exposure (credentials, documents, whiteboards, screens).
Check output/printer handling and screen locking.
Show that the exposed material provides direct value to an attacker.
Document the clean-desk baseline gap.

variants: Passwords on sticky notes.

mitigation: Define and enforce a clean-desk / information-handling baseline.
Provide secure storage and shredding; require clearing desks and whiteboards.
Use secure/pull printing to prevent unclaimed sensitive prints.
Enforce automatic screen locking.
Train staff on handling and run periodic clean-desk checks.
Discourage writing down credentials; provide a password manager.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Without a clean-desk rule, sensitive things pile up in the open — passwords on sticky notes, confidential printouts on desks, un-erased whiteboards — which a visitor or after-hours intruder can simply photograph. The fix is to set a clear clean-desk standard, provide secure storage, shredding, and pull-printing, require screens to lock automatically, and give staff a password manager so they don't write passwords down.

items.title: No Regular Phishing Susceptibility Assessment
items.prerequisites: Authorization to run a controlled phishing simulation and access to any prior phishing-test results. A phishing platform (gophish) and a target list agreed with the client.
items.whatItIs: Phishing is the leading initial-access vector, and the only way to measure an organization's susceptibility is to test it. If no regular, controlled phishing assessment is run, the organization has no data on how many staff would click, submit credentials, or run an attachment — and no way to target training. This assessment checks whether phishing susceptibility is measured over time.
items.rootCause: Phishing simulations require tooling, coordination, and care, so they are skipped or run once for compliance. Without a cadence, susceptibility is unmeasured and training is untargeted.
items.impact: Unmeasured susceptibility means the organization cannot quantify its most likely breach path, cannot prioritize training, and repeats the same weaknesses. Attackers exploit exactly the click-through the org never measured.
items.realWorldContext: Phishing is behind a large share of real breaches, and organizations that test regularly drive click rates down measurably over time, while those that never test have no idea how exposed they are. A phishing-assessment cadence turns the top breach vector from a blind spot into a managed, trending metric.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether controlled phishing assessments are run and how often.
Check whether results (click, submit, report rates) are tracked over time.
Assess whether results feed targeted training and risk assessment.
With authorization, run a coordinated phishing simulation.
Measure click, credential-submission, and reporting rates.
Document the assessment-cadence gap and current susceptibility.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization and scope for a controlled phishing simulation.
Review prior phishing-assessment history and metrics.
Design and send a benign, clearly-tracked phishing simulation via the platform.
Measure click, submission, and report rates.
Compare to any historical data (or note its absence).
Document susceptibility and the cadence/training gap.

variants: No phishing assessment ever run.
One-off compliance test with no trending.
No credential-harvesting variant tested.
Results collected but never used for training.
mitigation: Run regular, controlled phishing assessments with tracked metrics.
Trend click, submission, and report rates over time.
Feed results into targeted training and risk assessment.
Provide and promote an easy 'report phishing' mechanism.

items.rootCause: Phone calls carry no inherent identity proof, and staff default to being helpful. Without a verification requirement, a confident pretext is enough to extract information.
items.impact: Disclosed information over the phone (credentials, internal detail, verification data) enables account takeover, further pretexting, and fraud, exploiting a trusted channel that provides no real caller assurance.
items.realWorldContext: Vishing — a confident call with a plausible story — reliably extracts sensitive information from staff who have no way to verify the caller and every incentive to help. Requiring caller verification before disclosure over the phone is the control that turns 'sounds legitimate' into 'proven legitimate'.

items.title: No Callback Verification for Sensitive or Financial Requests
items.prerequisites: Authorization to assess (and coordinated-test) the verification process for sensitive/financial requests. Access to review the process.
items.whatItIs: High-risk requests — payments, bank-detail changes, credential resets, access grants — arriving by email or phone should be verified via an independent callback to a known contact before action. items.rootCause: Callback verification adds friction, so it is skipped for speed, especially under manufactured urgency. Requests are actioned on the originating (spoofable) channel alone.
items.impact: Without callback verification, forged payment/bank-change requests (BEC) and pressured reset/access requests are actioned, causing financial loss and account compromise, because the spoofable channel is trusted on its own.
items.realWorldContext: Business email compromise thrives on the absence of callback verification: a spoofed 'CEO' or 'supplier' email requesting an urgent payment or bank-detail change is actioned because no one called a known number to check. Mandatory out-of-band callback for sensitive requests is the single most effective control against this multi-billion-dollar fraud.

items.title: Confidential Conversations Audible in Public / Shared Areas

items.whatItIs: Sensitive information is often discussed where it can be overheard — reception, open-plan areas, lifts, cafes near the office, or meeting rooms with poor sound isolation. items.impact: Overheard conversations leak credentials, deal details, internal structure, and plans, feeding pretexting and providing intelligence with no technical attack — obtained by a nearby listener or waiting visitor.
items.realWorldContext: Shoulder-surfing's audible cousin — overhearing sensitive conversations in reception, lifts, or nearby cafes — is a low-tech intelligence source assessors use regularly, from deal terms to spoken passwords. Defining where sensitive conversations may happen, and isolating meeting rooms, closes this quiet leak.

items.realWorldContext: Voicemail systems with default or guessable PINs have been abused to intercept reset codes and sensitive messages, and callers routinely leave account details and callback numbers assuming privacy. items.title: No Protection Against Pretext-Based Information Disclosure

items.whatItIs: Pretexting — a fabricated scenario that makes disclosure seem reasonable ('I'm from IT and need to confirm your details', 'this is the auditor') — extracts information across phone, email, and chat. items.impact: Successful pretexting extracts credentials, internal information, and verification details across channels, feeding account takeover and further attacks — because the fabricated authority is trusted without verification.
items.realWorldContext: Pretexting is the engine of social engineering: a believable role and scenario ('IT support', 'the auditor', 'facilities') makes almost any request seem reasonable. Assessors extract information across phone, email, and chat this way routinely — which is why verification that holds regardless of the story is the real defence.

items.title: Staff Act on Unverified Email Instructions (BEC)
items.prerequisites: Authorization to run a coordinated BEC-style test and access to review request-handling and email-authentication controls.
items.whatItIs: Business Email Compromise (BEC) uses a spoofed or compromised email — often impersonating an executive or supplier — to instruct staff to make payments, change details, or share data. If staff act on such instructions without verifying integrity/authenticity, and if email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) is weak, BEC succeeds. This assessment checks resistance to acting on unverified email instructions.
items.rootCause: Email is trusted implicitly, executive/supplier authority discourages questioning, and email authentication is often weak — so spoofed or compromised instructions are actioned without integrity verification.
items.impact: Actioned BEC instructions cause direct financial loss, fraudulent bank-detail changes, and data disclosure, exploiting trust in email and the reluctance to question apparent authority.
items.realWorldContext: BEC is among the costliest cybercrimes by reported losses, and it works through pure social engineering over email — a spoofed executive or supplier and an urgent instruction. Verification procedures plus strong email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) are what stop an unverified email from moving money.

items.impact: A fraudulent bank-detail change redirects supplier or payroll payments to the attacker, causing direct and often large financial loss, exploiting the missing integrity verification.
items.realWorldContext: Redirected-payment fraud — a fake 'we've changed our bank details' request actioned without verification — is one of the most damaging BEC variants, with individual losses often large. Independent verification and dual control on bank-detail changes is the control that directly stops the money leaving.

items.realWorldContext: Fake-invoice and vendor-impersonation fraud costs organizations heavily every year, succeeding wherever invoices are paid without matching them to real orders and verified suppliers. The fix is to verify high-stakes requests by process — a callback to a known number, a shared code word, or two-person approval — regardless of who they appear to come from, and train staff that a familiar voice or face can now be faked.

items.title: Tailgating Through Access-Controlled Doors
items.prerequisites: Authorization to attempt tailgating at access-controlled entrances, and observation access. Physical presence at the site.
items.whatItIs: Access-controlled doors only work if one badge admits one person. Tailgating — following an authorized person through a door before it closes — defeats badge control entirely, and social norms (holding the door) make it easy. This tests whether physical access enforcement resists tailgating.
items.rootCause: Badge readers enforce one credential per unlock but cannot stop a second person walking through, and politeness discourages challenging followers. Without anti-tailgating measures and awareness, the control is bypassed.
items.impact: Tailgating gives an attacker facility access with no credential, bypassing all badge-based controls and enabling device theft, rogue-device placement, and access to sensitive areas.
items.realWorldContext: Tailgating is the single most reliable physical-intrusion technique in assessments — people hold doors open out of courtesy, and challenging a follower feels rude. Anti-tailgating measures plus a culture of polite challenge are what actually stop credential-free entry.

Check whether tailgating would be detected (cameras reviewed, alerts).
Document the access-enforcement gap.

Assess whether the tailgating was detected or challenged.

items.mitigationClientFacing: Badge-controlled doors only protect you if one badge lets one person in, but 'tailgating' — following someone through before the door closes — defeats that, and people hold doors open to be polite. The fix is to use physical measures like turnstiles or mantraps at sensitive doors, train staff to politely check unfamiliar followers and not hold secure doors, and watch entrances with cameras.

items.title: Shared or Cloned Access Badges

items.whatItIs: Access control assumes each badge belongs to one person and cannot be duplicated. When staff share badges for convenience, or when badges use cloneable low-frequency technology, access can be duplicated and misattributed. This tests whether badge access enforcement resists sharing and cloning.
items.rootCause: Badge sharing is convenient (a forgotten badge, a quick favour), and older 125kHz badges are trivially cloneable. Without policy enforcement and modern badge technology, one credential can become many.
items.impact: Shared/cloned badges let unauthorized people gain access under someone else's identity, defeating accountability and enabling an attacker with a cloned badge to enter as a legitimate holder.
items.realWorldContext: Low-frequency (125kHz) badges can be cloned in seconds with a cheap Proxmark from a brief brush past someone, and badge-sharing is rampant — both turn 'one badge, one person' into a fiction. Modern encrypted badge technology and anti-sharing enforcement are what restore real access control.

items.mitigationClientFacing: Access control assumes one badge belongs to one person and can't be copied — but staff share badges, and old-style badges can be cloned in seconds with cheap gear. items.title: Sensitive Areas Lack Additional Access Restriction
items.prerequisites: Authorization to assess access to sensitive areas (server rooms, executive offices, records) and review access levels.
items.whatItIs: Not all areas carry equal risk: server rooms, executive offices, and records storage warrant stricter access than general office space. If sensitive areas rely on the same broad badge access as everywhere else, far too many people can enter them. This tests whether sensitive areas apply least-privilege physical access.
items.rootCause: Access is often granted broadly for convenience, and sensitive areas are not separately restricted. Without least-privilege zoning, general access implies sensitive access.
items.impact: Over-broad access to sensitive areas lets many staff — and anyone who obtains a general badge — reach servers, executive information, or records, greatly expanding who can steal data or plant devices.
items.realWorldContext: Assessments routinely find that a general staff badge opens the server room or records store, because sensitive areas were never separately restricted. Applying least privilege to physical zones — so only those who need it can enter — is what contains the impact of a lost, shared, or cloned badge.

mitigation: Apply least-privilege access zoning: restrict sensitive areas to those who need them.
Require a second factor (PIN/biometric) for the most sensitive areas.

items.mitigationClientFacing: Some areas — server rooms, executive offices, records — are more sensitive than a general office and should be harder to enter, but often the same badge opens everything. The fix is to restrict sensitive areas to only the people who need them, add a PIN or fingerprint for the most sensitive ones, and regularly review who can get in.

items.title: Unattended Unlocked Workstations Enable Walk-Up Access
items.prerequisites: Authorization to observe and (in scope) interact with unattended workstations, and site access. A test USB device if permitted.
items.whatItIs: An unlocked, unattended workstation gives anyone walking by full access to a logged-in user's session — email, files, systems — with no credentials needed. If screens do not lock automatically and staff do not lock on leaving, walk-up access is trivial. This tests whether device-lock controls prevent walk-up session access.
items.rootCause: Automatic screen locking is often not enforced or set too long, and staff forget to lock when stepping away. The logged-in session then sits open to anyone nearby.
items.impact: Walk-up access to an unlocked session lets an attacker read/exfiltrate data, send email as the user, install a payload, or plant a device — a full session takeover with no authentication.
items.realWorldContext: Walking up to an unlocked, unattended workstation and acting as the logged-in user is a classic physical-assessment move that works constantly — a few minutes at an open session can plant a payload or exfiltrate data. Enforced auto-lock plus a lock-on-leave habit is the simple control that closes it.

items.mitigationClientFacing: An unlocked computer left unattended lets anyone walking by use the logged-in person's session — their email, files, and systems — with no password. The fix is to make screens lock automatically after a short idle time, remind staff to lock when they step away, and limit what plugged-in USB devices can do. The result is that a walk-up attacker finds locked, unattended machines rather than an open session they can immediately abuse.

items.title: Help-Desk Identity Verification Bypassed via Personal Data
items.prerequisites: Authorization to run a coordinated vishing test against help-desk identity verification, and OSINT-gathered personal data about a test target (with consent).
items.whatItIs: Help desks verify identity before resets or access changes, but if verification relies on knowledge an attacker can gather (name, employee ID, date of birth, manager) rather than something only the real user has, it is easily bypassed. This tests whether help-desk identity verification resists an attacker armed with personal data.
items.rootCause: Verification questions often use 'personal' data that is actually discoverable via OSINT or breaches. Without strong, non-guessable verification, a well-researched attacker answers them and passes.
items.impact: Bypassed verification lets an attacker reset a target's password or re-enroll MFA, taking over the account — a direct account-takeover path exploiting weak, knowledge-based verification.
items.realWorldContext: Attackers research a target's personal details from social media and breach data, then answer the help desk's 'security questions' to trigger a reset — a technique behind real account-takeover and SIM-swap incidents. Verification that relies on discoverable knowledge is verification an attacker can pass.

Assess whether stronger verification (out-of-band, one-time codes) is used.
Document the identity-verification gap.

items.mitigationClientFacing: Help desks check who you are before resetting passwords, but if they rely on facts a scammer can find online (your name, ID, date of birth), that check is easily beaten. The fix is to verify people using something only the real user has — like a one-time code sent to their registered device — confirm sensitive changes with the real user, and apply extra checks for important accounts.

items.title: SIM-Swap Enables SMS-Based MFA Bypass
items.prerequisites: Authorization to assess reliance on SMS-based MFA and account-recovery, and (in scope) coordinated testing of the recovery process. Process review access.
items.whatItIs: SMS-based MFA and phone-number-based account recovery can be defeated by a SIM-swap: an attacker convinces (or bribes) a mobile carrier to move the victim's number to their SIM, then receives the victim's SMS codes. This tests whether the organization's reliance on phone-number-based authentication exposes it to SIM-swap account takeover.
items.rootCause: SMS MFA and phone-based recovery are convenient and widely deployed, but the phone number's security depends on the carrier, which social engineering can defeat. Reliance on it inherits that weakness.
items.impact: A successful SIM-swap lets an attacker receive MFA codes and recovery messages, taking over accounts protected only by SMS — a well-documented account-takeover path, especially for high-value targets.
items.realWorldContext: SIM-swap attacks have driven high-profile account takeovers and cryptocurrency thefts, defeating SMS-based MFA by moving the victim's number to the attacker. Because the weakness lives at the carrier, any account relying on SMS codes or phone-based recovery inherits it — which is why phishing-resistant MFA matters.

Assess reliance on the phone number as an authentication factor.
Consider the SIM-swap threat for high-value accounts.

Assess availability of phishing-resistant MFA alternatives.
Document the SMS/phone-reliance exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization and coordination for any recovery-process test.
Map where SMS MFA and phone-based recovery are used.
Assess whether a SIM-swap would grant account access via SMS codes.
Coordinate a controlled test of the recovery process's phone reliance.
Assess phishing-resistant MFA availability and adoption.

items.title: Sensitive Documents Not Securely Destroyed

If secure destruction is not enforced, recoverable sensitive documents leave the building. This tests whether sensitive document disposal prevents recovery.
items.rootCause: Secure destruction adds friction and cost, so documents go into ordinary recycling. Without enforced disposal and provided shredding, sensitive material is recoverable.
items.impact: Recovered sensitive documents expose customer data, internal information, and sometimes credentials directly, enabling fraud, pretexting, and reconnaissance with no technical attack.
items.realWorldContext: Dumpster-diving for sensitive documents remains effective because secure destruction is inconsistently enforced — assessors and real intruders alike recover customer records and internal memos from ordinary recycling. items.realWorldContext: USB-drop attacks (leaving infected drives for curious staff to plug in) and data leaks from lost unencrypted drives are both well-documented. Controlling USB use, encrypting portable media, and sanitizing it before disposal is what closes this two-way channel.

items.prerequisites: Authorization to assess the facility perimeter and entry points, and site access for observation. Physical presence.
items.whatItIs: The facility perimeter and its entry points — main doors, side/service entrances, loading docks, fire exits, windows — are the first physical control. Weaknesses (propped doors, unmonitored side entrances, accessible fire exits, ground-floor windows) let an attacker bypass reception entirely. This tests whether the perimeter and all entry points are adequately secured.
items.rootCause: Perimeter security focuses on the main entrance, and secondary entry points (service doors, fire exits, windows) are overlooked or propped open for convenience. Attackers target the weakest point, not the front door.
items.impact: An inadequately-secured entry point lets an attacker enter unnoticed, bypassing reception and badge control, and reach sensitive areas, devices, and documents.
items.realWorldContext: Physical red-teams routinely bypass a well-guarded front entrance by using a propped service door, an accessible fire exit, or a ground-floor window — the perimeter is only as strong as its weakest point. Securing and monitoring all entry points, not just the main door, is what closes these bypasses.
stepsToIdentify: Survey the perimeter and all entry points (main, side/service, loading dock, fire exits, windows).
Identify propped doors, unmonitored entrances, and accessible windows.

items.mitigationClientFacing: The weakest way into a building is often not the front door but a propped side door, an unwatched service entrance, an accessible fire exit, or a ground-floor window. The fix is to secure and monitor every entry point, stop doors from being propped open (with alarms if needed), make sure fire exits can't be used to get in, and secure accessible windows.
